transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. Could you start by telling me what brings you in to see me today?

I came in because even on my better days, I can’t shake this feeling that people at church and in my walking club are watching me. Sometimes it feels like they put little messages about me in the church bulletin, or in things they say.
Have you noticed any periods where you felt unusually sad, hopeless, or low - or the opposite, unusually energetic, elated, or irritable - around the same time you've been feeling watched?

Yes. When I was at my lowest, I was barely eating and felt like I’d failed everyone. That was also when I was hearing my friend’s voice and thinking the people at church were sending messages about me.
Aside from those low periods, have you ever felt watched or heard that voice when your mood was otherwise normal, not particularly low or high?

Yes. There was a stretch of a few weeks when I was getting dressed and eating a little better, and I didn’t feel so weighed down. But I still heard my name in the house, and I still thought people at church were hinting about me.
Thinking back to when this all started, how many months or years ago did you first begin feeling watched or hearing your name called?
It started about eleven months ago, I think. The voices, the messages, and having trouble keeping my thoughts straight—all of that has been going on since then.
Over these past eleven months, would you say the times you felt watched or heard your name—without any low mood or high energy—lasted for more than half of that entire time, or was it less than half?
It was less than half, I think. There was that spell of several weeks when I was doing a little better, but I still heard my name and felt like people at church were hinting about me.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient demonstrates a concurrent major mood episode (depressive, with poor appetite and feelings of failure/hopelessness) together with psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations of her name being called, and delusional beliefs that church/walking club members were sending hidden messages about her). Critically, she also experienced a multi-week period during which the psychotic symptoms (hallucinations and referential delusions) persisted in the absence of a full mood episode, satisfying the requirement for psychotic symptoms occurring independent of mood disturbance for at least 2 weeks. However, over the total ~11 month illness course, the psychotic-only period was less than half of the total duration, meaning mood symptoms were present for the majority of the illness course. This pattern—concurrent psychotic and mood symptoms, a discrete period of psychosis without mood symptoms, and mood symptoms occurring for the majority of the illness duration—is diagnostic of Schizoaffective Disorder (F25) rather than Schizophrenia (F20, which would require psychotic symptoms predominating with mood symptoms brief/incidental) or a Mood Disorder with Psychotic Features (F32.3, which would require psychotic symptoms to occur only during mood episodes).

confirmed_symptoms: Auditory hallucinations (hearing her name called, hearing her friend's voice)
Delusions of reference (belief that church bulletin and members' comments contained hidden messages about her)
Persecutory ideation (feeling watched by people at church and walking club)
Depressed mood with feelings of failure/hopelessness
Mood symptoms co-occurring with psychotic symptoms during the low period
Several-week period of improved mood/eating with persistence of auditory hallucinations and referential delusions
